addmaths-0606-vectors-components.description: Read a column vector, reverse a displacement and combine horizontal and vertical components.

sections.title: What do two components tell me?
sections.label: Direction

blocks.html: A column vector records two signed moves. The top entry is the horizontal move and the bottom entry is the vertical move.

figure.alt: An arrow from A to B with dotted horizontal and vertical legs, labelled horizontal and vertical moves.
figure.caption: The horizontal and vertical moves add to the displacement from A to B.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Start on a set of axes. Count one component at a time. Positive horizontal means right and positive vertical means up. The figure draws the separate moves as dotted lines. The arrow connects the same starting and finishing points. \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) goes from A to B. \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) returns from B to A and has both signs reversed. The numbers in the vector describe the move, so a copy of the same arrow starting elsewhere describes the same vector.

blocks.title: End position minus start position
blocks.prompt: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}24\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}36\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
blocks.hint: Write the destination first. Check the direction by adding the result to the start position.
blocks.solution:
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}36\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}24\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: The components describe the reverse journey. Subtract the position of A from the position of B.

blocks.html: The bottom entry gives a vertical displacement. It only gives a y-coordinate when the arrow starts at the origin.

blocks.title: Recover a starting position
blocks.prompt: After 3 equal displacements of \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-3\end{pmatrix}\), a marker arrives at \(\begin{pmatrix}43\\-13\end{pmatrix}\). Give the starting position as a column vector.
blocks.hint: Work backwards from the final position using the opposite of the total displacement.
blocks.solution:
The total displacement is \(\begin{pmatrix}15\\-9\end{pmatrix}\).

The arrival position is the start plus total displacement, so subtract the displacement from \(\begin{pmatrix}43\\-13\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}28\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

blocks.html: If a vector points in the wrong direction, reverse both signs and check the start and finish.

sections.title: How do I add, subtract or scale a vector?
sections.label: Operations

blocks.html: Add or subtract matching entries. Scaling multiplies both entries by the same number.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Draw the first arrow. Put the tail of the next arrow at the first arrowhead. The resultant runs from the initial tail to the final arrowhead. A negative multiplier reverses direction as well as changing size. To subtract, put the arrow in reverse before adding it. On paper, draw the arrows first when their order is easy to confuse. Multiply any scalar before adding or subtracting the two columns.

blocks.title: Combine two directions
blocks.prompt: Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}29\\-5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\31\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(4\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).
blocks.hint: Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.
blocks.solution:
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}116\\-20\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}-8\\31\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}124\\-51\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: This is the result when the second vector is added. Reverse both of its components before adding.

blocks.html: Multiplying only one component will usually change the angle. Keep the same scale factor in both components.

blocks.title: End position minus start position
blocks.prompt: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}33\\-9\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}43\\-12\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
blocks.hint: Write the destination first. Check the direction by adding the result to the start position.
blocks.solution:
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}43\\-12\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}33\\-9\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: The components describe the reverse journey. Subtract the position of A from the position of B.

blocks.html: If a vector points in the wrong direction, reverse both signs and check the start and finish.

blocks.title: Read i and j
blocks.html: \(\mathbf i=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf j=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}\). In \(a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j\), the horizontal component is \(a\) and the vertical component is \(b\).

blocks.title: Find the second move
blocks.prompt: The total displacement is \(5\mathbf i-3\mathbf j\) metres. The first move is \(-2\mathbf i+\mathbf j\) metres. Find the second move. Use \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j\) or give its ordered components.
blocks.hint: Subtract the first move from the total. Subtracting \(-2\mathbf i\) increases the horizontal component.
blocks.solution: \((5-(-2))\mathbf i+(-3-1)\mathbf j=7\mathbf i-4\mathbf j\). The robot moves 7 metres to the right and 4 metres down in the second move.

retry.feedback: This adds the first move to the total. Subtract it to recover the second move.

sections.title: How can I recover a missing entry?
sections.label: Matching

blocks.html: Two column vectors are equal exactly when both matching entries are equal.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Copy the two columns on opposite sides of the page. Read across each row to build two scalar equations. If a row has no unknown, it gives a quick check of signs. In a journey, the same comparison works for the initial position plus a number of equal displacements. After finding a parameter in one row, put it back into the other row before you finish.

blocks.title: Match the bottom components
blocks.prompt: \(\begin{pmatrix}34\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(5\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-3\\39\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}173\\-89\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).
blocks.hint: Equate bottom entries. Solve the value before checking the other entry.
blocks.solution:
The bottom entry gives \(5p-(39)=-89\).

Add \(39\) and divide both sides by \(5\).

Answer: \(-10\).

blocks.html: Adding the two components together does not test equality. Equal totals can come from different arrows.

The arrival position is the start plus total displacement, so subtract the displacement from \(\begin{pmatrix}50\\-23\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}38\\-14\end{pmatrix}\).

addmaths-0606-vectors-length.description: Use a right triangle to find a magnitude, a direction vector of length one or a required signed component.

sections.title: Why is finding the length a right-triangle problem?
sections.label: Magnitude

blocks.html: The two components form the perpendicular legs, so the length rule is \(\left|\mathbf v\right|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\).

figure.alt: An arrow from A to B with dotted horizontal and vertical legs, labelled horizontal and vertical moves.
figure.caption: The horizontal and vertical moves add to the displacement from A to B.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Mark the legs parallel to the axes. A leg length is always positive, even when the arrow points left or down. Squaring already removes a negative sign, provided it is inside brackets. Keep exact square roots for surds. The denominator in the normalising factor in the next model is this same length.

Question asks forUseful operation
The displacement between two pointsFinish minus start: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}\)
The length of a vector\(\left|\mathbf v\right|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\)
A unit vector in the same direction\(\widehat{\mathbf v}=\frac{\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|}\)

blocks.title: Measure the length of an arrow
blocks.prompt: Find the magnitude of \(\begin{pmatrix}387\\-1720\end{pmatrix}\).
blocks.hint: A displacement component can be negative. Both squared contributions to a length are non-negative.
blocks.solution:
The legs of the component triangle have lengths \(387\) and \(1720\).

The square of the length is \(387^2+(-1720)^2=3108169\).

Take the positive square root.

Answer: \(1763\).

retry.feedback: Adding the lengths gives the route along the legs. The vector is the direct diagonal.

blocks.html: Adding the two component lengths gives a route along the sides of the triangle. The vector length runs across the diagonal.

blocks.title: Find a specified component from a magnitude
blocks.prompt: The magnitude of \(\begin{pmatrix}368\\q\end{pmatrix}\) is \(782\) and its second component is negative. Find \(q\).
blocks.hint: A squared component has two candidate signs. Read the direction before choosing one.
blocks.solution:
Use \((368)^2+q^2=611524\).

This gives \(q^2=476100\). The stated direction selects the negative value.

Answer: \(-690\).

retry.feedback: Both signs give the correct length. The question requires a negative second component.

blocks.html: Use brackets around negative components when you square them.

sections.title: How can I keep only the direction?
sections.label: Unit

blocks.html: Divide by the magnitude to make the length one: \(\widehat{\mathbf v}=\frac{\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|}\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: The vector from its tail to its tip points in the required direction. Find its magnitude with Pythagoras. Dividing by that positive length scales the arrow down or up to unit length. Keep two exact fractions in the column vector. Check the result by squaring and adding the two new entries. The basis vectors \(\mathbf i\) and \(\mathbf j\) are unit vectors along the positive horizontal and vertical axes.

blocks.title: A unit vector in the same direction
blocks.prompt: Find a unit vector in the direction of \(\begin{pmatrix}-322\\-1104\end{pmatrix}\).
blocks.hint: Use the magnitude as the divisor for both components.
blocks.solution:
The magnitude of the given vector is \(1150\).

Divide each component by \(1150\). The scale factor is positive, so the arrow keeps its direction.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{7}{25}\\-\frac{24}{25}\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: This arrow has unit length but is pointing the opposite way.

blocks.html: A vector of length one can point in any direction. Check the signs against the original arrow.

blocks.title: Choose a vector of the required length
blocks.prompt: Find the vector with magnitude \(1287\) that points in the same direction as \(\begin{pmatrix}-240\\-576\end{pmatrix}\).
blocks.hint: Think of the original vector in two steps: first give it length one, then give it the requested length.
blocks.solution:
Divide the original vector by \(624\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{5}{13}\\-\frac{12}{13}\end{pmatrix}\) of length one.

Multiply the resulting vector by \(1287\) for the required length.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}-495\\-1188\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: The length is right but the direction is opposite.

blocks.html: Use brackets around negative components when you square them.

sections.title: What if a length is given instead?
sections.label: Target

blocks.html: Scale a unit direction by the requested length. If one component is missing, solve for its square and use the direction to choose its sign.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For a reverse calculation, put the length squared on one side and both squared components on the other. Isolate the square of the unknown. Both square-root signs are possible until a direction restriction fixes one. When a full direction is given, the unit-vector method avoids working with the two signs separately.

Multiply the resulting vector by \(1819\) for the required length.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}856\\-1605\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: The length is right but the direction is opposite.

blocks.html: The magnitude does not distinguish upward from downward. Read the stated sign or quadrant before deciding.

addmaths-0606-vectors-ratios.description: Find a midpoint or dividing point with a position vector and interpret positions beyond a segment.

sections.title: How far along a line is the dividing point?
sections.label: Fraction

blocks.html: For \(AC:CB=r:s\), the distance from A to C is the fraction \(\frac{r}{r+s}\) of the full distance.

figure.alt: Four equally spaced collinear points A, B, C and D, with an arrow from A to D.
figure.caption: The same start point can reach B, C or D by scaling the direction to C.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Mark the start, target and finish. Treat the whole arrow as all the parts, not just the parts still to go. Multiply the displacement by the required fraction. Because this is a displacement from A, add the position of A afterwards to obtain the position from the origin. revision.body:
How far along a line is the dividing point?

For \(AC:CB=r:s\), the distance from A to C is the fraction \(\frac{r}{r+s}\) of the full distance.

What happens outside the segment?

A scale above \(1\) carries a point past the target. A negative scale places it on the other side of the start.

addmaths-0606-vectors-lines.description: Compare direction vectors, prove collinearity and find the meeting position of intersecting lines.

sections.title: Do two arrows have the same line direction?
sections.label: Parallel

blocks.html: Two non-zero directions are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other.

figure.alt: Two arrows lie on parallel lines. One points down and right, and the other points up and left.
figure.caption: Multiplying a non-zero vector by a negative scalar reverses its direction and leaves its line parallel.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Find the scalar from a pair of non-zero components. Apply it to the second entries and compare. A negative factor is allowed because it gives an antiparallel direction. If both first entries are zero, use the second entries. If only one first entry is zero, the vectors cannot be aligned unless one whole vector is zero.

blocks.title: Compare corresponding components
blocks.prompt: Find \(p\) such that \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\-3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}14\\p\end{pmatrix}\) are parallel.
blocks.hint: Parallel vectors may point in opposite directions. Keep the sign of the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
The first entries determine the scalar multiplier \(2\).

Multiply the second entry \(-3\) by the same scalar.

Answer: \(-6\).

blocks.html: Parallel directions can point the opposite way. The test is a common scalar and the sign can be negative.

blocks.title: Combine two directions
blocks.prompt: Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}67\\-5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-12\\69\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(2\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).
blocks.hint: Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.
blocks.solution:
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}134\\-10\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}-12\\69\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}146\\-79\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: This is the result when the second vector is added. Reverse both of its components before adding.

blocks.html: A collinearity proof needs a common point as well as a parallel direction.

sections.title: When are three points on the same line?
sections.label: Same line

blocks.html: Compare two non-zero displacements with a common starting point. If one is a scalar multiple of the other, the three points are collinear.

figure.alt: Four equally spaced collinear points A, B, C and D, with an arrow from A to D.
figure.caption: The same start point can reach B, C or D by scaling the direction to C.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: From three positions, subtract the position of A from the other two. This gives \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and the displacement from A to C. Show the same multiplier works horizontally and vertically. Both arrows pass through A, so their parallel directions put all three points on one line. If the directions come from separate origins, parallel arrows alone cannot prove the lines coincide.

blocks.title: Check whether three points lie on a line

blocks.hint: Compare two displacements that share a starting point. Use both components.
blocks.solution:
The routes from A are \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}60\\-15\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}24\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

Both components have the same ratio. The two vectors have the same start, so the points are collinear.

Answer: Yes, they are collinear.

retry.feedback: Use the ratio from one component to predict the other, then check it.

blocks.html: Comparing the distance from the origin alone does not test whether three points lie on one line.

Answer: \(21\).

sections.title: How do I meet a second route?
sections.label: Crossing

blocks.html: At a crossing, two journeys lead to exactly the same position. Their separate journey lengths can differ.

figure.alt: Two different straight trajectories cross at a point C. Both arrows show the directions of motion.
figure.caption: Both robots must reach the crossing at the same time for a collision.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Write each position as start plus a multiple of its direction. Use different letters for the two multiples, such as \(r\) and \(s\). Equate first components and then second components. Solve the two scalar equations by elimination. Put one parameter into the route that uses it and use the other route to verify the final column vector.

blocks.title: Match positions on two lines
blocks.prompt: One line contains the points \(\begin{pmatrix}73\\-11\end{pmatrix}+r\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). The other contains \(\begin{pmatrix}73\\-\frac{55}{2}\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(r\) at the intersection.
blocks.hint: Set one equation per component. Do not assume the two line parameters are the same.
blocks.solution:
Equate top and bottom entries separately. The displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\-\frac{33}{2}\end{pmatrix}\) equals \(r\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\end{pmatrix}-s\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}\).

Eliminate \(s\) by cross-multiplying its two coefficients. The compatible second parameter is \(3\).

Answer: \(\frac{3}{2}\).

retry.feedback: That is the parameter of the second line. Substitute for it to find the first parameter.

blocks.html: Using one letter for both route parameters can force an extra condition. The positions agree, but the journey lengths need not.

blocks.title: Find where two routes cross
blocks.prompt: Line positions are \(\begin{pmatrix}77\\-15\end{pmatrix}+r\begin{pmatrix}10\\-7\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{320}{3}\\-\frac{301}{6}\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}4\\8\end{pmatrix}\). Give the position vector where the lines meet.
blocks.hint: The parameters belong to different lines. Solve by equating positions and substitute into one expression.
blocks.solution:
Compare both components at once. Solving the linear equations gives \(r=\frac{7}{2},\ s=\frac{4}{3}\).

Put either parameter back into its own expression to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}112\\-\frac{79}{2}\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}112\\-\frac{79}{2}\end{pmatrix}\).

revision.body:
Do two arrows have the same line direction?

Two non-zero directions are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other.

When are three points on the same line?

Compare two non-zero displacements with a common starting point. If one is a scalar multiple of the other, the three points are collinear.

How do I meet a second route?

At a crossing, two journeys lead to exactly the same position. Their separate journey lengths can differ.

blocks.title: Practise the method

sections.title: How do I reach a position after a time?

blocks.html: For constant velocity, displacement equals elapsed time multiplied by velocity. Add the start to get a position.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Check the units first. In \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), multiply by the time in seconds to get a displacement in metres. To compare two moving objects, use the time measured from the same instant. Read across the columns to get the equation in each coordinate. Use the row with a non-zero difference in velocities to identify the candidate collision time.

blocks.title: Move a starting position for a fixed time
blocks.prompt: A raft starts at \(\begin{pmatrix}81\\0\end{pmatrix}\) metres. Its velocity relative to the water is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-93\end{pmatrix}\) and the current is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\87\end{pmatrix}\) in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the position after 9 seconds.
blocks.hint: Add the velocity components first. Multiply by the time to get a displacement.
blocks.solution:
Ground velocity is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\). The displacement after 9 seconds is \(\begin{pmatrix}27\\-54\end{pmatrix}\).

Add the displacement to the starting position \(\begin{pmatrix}81\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}108\\-54\end{pmatrix}\).

blocks.html: Equal horizontal positions only guarantee that the objects are level in one direction. Check the vertical positions too.

blocks.title: Find when two moving objects meet
blocks.prompt: Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}85\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}121\\-121\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\-5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\8\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. After how many seconds do they meet?
blocks.hint: Compare both positions at the same time. One component can give a candidate time, but it must work in the other.
blocks.solution:
At a meeting, \(\begin{pmatrix}85\\-4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}7\\-5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}121\\-121\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\8\end{pmatrix}\).

Using the horizontal entries gives \(t=9\). Both equations agree because \(9\begin{pmatrix}4\\-13\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}36\\-117\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(9\).

sections.title: When is a crossing a collision?
sections.label: Collision

blocks.html: A collision needs the same place at the same time, with a non-negative time counted from the given start.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Solve the two component equations independently when both relative velocity components are non-zero. If the candidate times differ, the routes cross at different times or they do not meet. If a component has equal velocities, compare initial positions for that coordinate. Equal starts make that equation true for all times. Unequal starts make a meeting impossible.

blocks.title: Locate the meeting point
blocks.prompt: Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}86\\-5\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}126\\-155\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\-6\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\9\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. Find their meeting position.
blocks.hint: A meeting position is the initial position plus the velocity multiplied by the common time.
blocks.solution:
The equation for equal positions gives a common time of 10 seconds. Both components satisfy it.

Substitute that time into the first position vector. This gives \(\begin{pmatrix}86\\-5\end{pmatrix}+10\begin{pmatrix}8\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}166\\-65\end{pmatrix}\).

blocks.html: A crossing drawn without times shows a shared point on the routes. It cannot confirm both objects reach it together.

blocks.title: Decide whether two moving objects meet
blocks.prompt: Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}90\\-9\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}230\\-163\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\6\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. Do the robots meet after the timing starts?
blocks.hint: Two routes can cross without a collision. Test whether the times agree as well.
blocks.solution:
The vertical equation gives \(t=14\). The horizontal equation gives \(t=14\).

The same non-negative time satisfies both equations.

Answer: Yes, at the same time.
